title: A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a hand interface that lets people manipulate digital or remote objects while reliably feeling their shape, resistance, texture, slip, and motion. It would coordinate tactile feedback—the sensations produced at the skin—with kinesthetic feedback, such as resistance to finger movement. These complementary capabilities would need to work together across multiple fingers and both hands while preserving comfortable movement. This describes the intended capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Scope definition: general purpose means useful across varied objects, materials, and manipulation tasks rather than a single programmed sensation or force-control exercise. High fidelity means that the feedback conveys relevant physical properties consistently enough to guide action, with forces delivered at the appropriate location and in the appropriate direction. The intended interface would avoid dependence on a bulky stationary machine. Thermal sensation and pain are optional extensions, not requirements for this concept.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would make physical properties available as a much richer medium for computer interaction. People could adjust a grip when an object begins to slip, feel how a simulated material yields, or regulate contact with a remote object using information supplied through their hands. The N2D study provides a limited technical basis for this reasoning: directional force feedback improved some measures of force regulation and user experience in a teleoperation experiment. Extending those benefits to diverse objects and sensations remains conditional on the proposed breakthrough.

Conditional impact synthesis: richer simulation and force-informed remote manipulation would follow directly from reliable physical feedback. Training, design, and collaborative manipulation could become more closely connected to the physical skills people already use. Remote surgery, manufacturing, and repair would require additional advances and validation in robots, sensing, communications, and application-specific safety. A convincing sensation at the hand would not by itself establish that a remote system can measure, reproduce, or safely act on the corresponding physical interaction.

Interpretive limit: describing physical interaction as a general computational medium is an analogy about an expanded interface capability. It does not imply that arbitrary digital objects could acquire every property of real matter, that simulated practice would always transfer to physical work, or that the interface would replace physical objects. The revolutionary judgment rests on the proposed combination of breadth, perceptual fidelity, and freedom of movement; a useful improvement in one force-feedback task establishes a narrower result.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is coordinated tactile and directional force feedback across the hand without unacceptable restrictions on movement, fit, or endurance. The supplied paper grounds this integration challenge by discussing complementary haptic capabilities and by identifying gaps among the systems its authors reviewed. That comparison supports the research goal but does not establish that every contemporary system has the same limitations or that these are the only barriers.

Concrete engineering barriers include extending directional coverage, coordinating feedback across multiple digits, accommodating individual hand geometry through fitting and calibration, and reducing wearable mass while retaining useful force delivery. N2D illustrates these tradeoffs: its three-finger design provides planar feedback, leaves the direction associated with finger adduction and abduction unreflected, requires user-specific calibration, and can become fatiguing during extended use. These are documented limitations of that device, not universal limits on haptic engineering.

Research-goal synthesis: a general interface would also need to coordinate changing contact locations and force directions so that shape, texture, slip, and compliance remain mutually consistent during manipulation. Increasing actuator coverage alone would not establish this perceptual result. The scientific and engineering challenge includes determining which combinations of cues support reliable perception and action across users and tasks, then delivering those cues with sustained comfort and safe behavior.

Alternative-route synthesis: direct nervous-system stimulation could be another route to artificial touch, but the supplied evidence does not establish its mechanisms, maturity, or remaining technical barriers. It is not a necessary component of HCI-03. Any assessment of that route would require separate neuroengineering evidence.

current_state.text: Yao-Ting Huang, Jake Honma, Omar Hernandez, and colleagues’ “The N2D Haptic Glove: A Multi-Finger Glove for 2D Directional Force Feedback for Contact Rich Manipulation,” dated 12 June 2026, is a preprint reporting benchtop validation and a 16-participant teleoperated scale-pressing study. It documents a relevant advance in directional force feedback. Its experiment does not establish general realism for shape, texture, compliance, slip, or varied two-handed manipulation.

The glove actuates three fingers and provides planar force feedback. It weighs 562 grams excluding its off-hand battery, and the authors identify fatigue during extended use as a limitation. Finger adduction and abduction are outside the reflected force direction. These details matter because the proposed innovation requires useful directional coverage and sustained usability as well as successful force rendering in a restricted task.

The teleoperation results show a bounded advantage. At the 100 g axial target, 2D feedback significantly improved force regulation relative to both visual-only and 1D feedback. The advantage over 1D feedback was not statistically significant at the 50 g axial target or in transverse probing. The result supports useful directional feedback under particular experimental conditions; it does not establish a uniform benefit across the tested conditions or demonstrate the full proposed interface.

The evidence available for this record consists of one paper and the supplied review of it. It cannot establish whether any other system achieves the proposed combination of range, fidelity, and freedom of movement. No bounded search record was supplied, so field-wide coverage through 1 November 2026 remains unresolved. That coverage limitation does not undermine the documented June 2026 findings or establish that the broader capability is impossible.

Access and interpretation limits: the supplied review reports access to the complete retained paper text and references, but the figures themselves were not inspected and some equations had conversion artifacts. The device specifications, study scope, statistical distinctions, and limitations summarized here come from the textual findings described in that review. This record does not add independent inspection or visual verification.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: evaluate varied two-handed tasks involving unfamiliar shapes, incipient slip, textures, and compliant materials. Compare task performance and perceived properties with both physical objects and existing haptic systems. Use blinded comparisons where feasible, and specify which conditions can actually be concealed from participants and evaluators. Success should involve multiple kinds of manipulation; a single force-rendering exercise would establish only that narrower capability.
completion_criteria.label: Varied two-handed manipulation benchmarked against physical objects and haptic systems

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility criteria: define task coverage, participant characteristics, fitting and calibration procedures, comparison conditions, outcome measures, and quantitative acceptance thresholds before evaluation. Report results by task and condition so that average improvements do not conceal important failures. Independent replication, including unfamiliar objects and users, would strengthen the case for generality. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined acceptance thresholds and results by task and condition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical criteria: demonstrate sustained comfort, movement freedom, and safe failure behavior across users and intended settings. Specify exposure durations, safety limits, and the operating envelope within which the interface delivers reliable feedback. Evaluate how calibration and fitting affect performance and usability. The documented N2D fatigue and calibration concerns motivate these tests, but the paper does not prescribe the proposed protocol or its acceptance thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained comfort, movement freedom, and safe failure across users

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundary: successful finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested tasks, users, and operating conditions, not literal universality or perfect equivalence to physical objects. Specialized remote applications would still need their own end-to-end validation. Thermal sensation and pain need not be demonstrated to satisfy the scope defined here.
completion_criteria.label: Claims limited to tested tasks, users, and operating conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could provide models for predicting haptic perception, learning, and task performance. HCI-03 concerns the resulting interaction capability and hardware; it could advance even while predictive theory remains incomplete.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-02, “Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis,” overlaps if artificial touch is incorporated into neural control systems. Its central outcome is communication and control after paralysis, whereas HCI-03 concerns tactile and force interaction. HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality,” overlaps when touch becomes an accessible input or output channel. Accessibility through a chosen modality does not itself require realistic physical feedback, and a high-fidelity haptic device would not automatically be accessible to every user.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” is complementary because spatial images and haptic feedback could describe the same digital object. Convincing visual depth does not establish convincing touch. HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” could incorporate shared haptic manipulation, but its collaboration outcome also depends on coordination and social cues beyond physical feedback.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-05, “End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain,” could help users author haptic interactions. HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” could use physical feedback during supervised remote manipulation. Their core breakthroughs concern understandable programming and meaningful control, respectively; neither is established by producing realistic forces or sensations.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” and HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” have more indirect relationships. Haptic cues might serve as an additional output channel, while sensing and recording hand interactions could create privacy or memory-design questions. These possible integrations do not make language translation, enforceable privacy, or evidence-controlled memory part of HCI-03’s completion criteria.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system achieves the proposed combined range, fidelity, and freedom of movement remains unresolved; no bounded field-wide search record was supplied.
The N2D findings remain preprint results. Independent replication or subsequent validation is not established by the supplied inputs.
A completion protocol still needs feasible blinding procedures, task coverage, exposure durations, safety limits, quantitative acceptance thresholds, and a defined practical operating envelope.
The mechanisms, maturity, and limitations of direct nervous-system stimulation require separate evidence if that optional route is developed.
Figures were not inspected in the supplied review, and some equations had conversion artifacts; conclusions requiring those materials remain outside this record’s verified scope.

brief.title: Hands that feel digital and distant objects
possible: You could handle a digital object with both hands and feel its shape, texture, resistance, and movement. You could sense it starting to slip or yielding under your grip, while moving comfortably without a bulky fixed machine.
When controlling a robot remotely, you could feel contact through your hands and adjust your grip or pressure. Sensations at the skin would work together with forces that resist or move your fingers.
why: Touch would give people richer information for acting on a computer or through a robot. Training, design, and shared manipulation could draw more directly on the physical skills people already use.

sources.who: Yao-Ting Huang, Jake Honma, Omar Hernandez and colleagues at UC San Diego
sources.showed: The N2D glove applies forces in a plane across several fingertips. In a remote robot-control study, it improved pressure control in some conditions compared with viewing alone or feeling force along a single direction.
sources.quote: planar fingertip feedback significantly reduces contact force error during precise manipulation, improves trial-to-trial consistency, and enhances overall user experience in axial probing tasks.
sources.cited_for: It supports the value of feeling force direction when controlling contact remotely.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate realistic shape, texture, slip, and resistance across varied tasks using both hands.

sources.who: Nicha Vanichvoranun, Hojeong Lee, Seoyeon Kim and Sang Ho Yoon
sources.showed: EStatiG combines brakes that resist movement at several finger segments with fingertip vibration. Users better perceived finger bending and reported greater realism when grasping virtual shapes.
sources.quote:
Our results showed a significant improvement in the perception of
phalanx angle positions and the overall experience of realism and immersion when interacting with various object shapes in
VR.
sources.cited_for: It supports distributing resistance along fingers to improve the perception of virtual objects.
sources.not_established: It does not establish freely directed forces and consistent touch across varied manipulation tasks.

sources.who: Pablo Alvarez Romeo and Mehmet Ercan Altinsoy
sources.showed: KinesCeTI fits different hand sizes and uses interchangeable mechanisms to resist or actively move the index finger and thumb. User studies assessed fit, feedback, and usability in real and virtual tasks.
sources.quote:
Results
indicate that the glove adapts to different hand sizes and
provides effective feedback with both mechanisms, highlighting
its potential as a versatile platform for haptic research.
sources.cited_for: It supports adaptable fit and interchangeable force mechanisms as practical parts of a hand interface.
sources.not_established: It addresses movement forces rather than skin sensations and does not demonstrate coordinated feedback across both hands.

sources.who: Siyeon Baik, Shinsuk Park and Jaeyoung Park
sources.showed: Their cable-driven glove combines skin contact with resistance at finger joints. Adding skin feedback improved sensitivity to contact force and its perceived realism.
sources.quote: The experimental result indicates that the availability of the cutaneous feedback significantly improved the perceived realism and acuity of the contact force.
sources.cited_for: It supports combining skin sensations with resistance to finger movement.
sources.not_established: The glove serves the thumb and index finger; it does not establish the full range of sensations during varied manipulation.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated useful pieces of this capability. Huang and colleagues tested N2D with 16 participants. Its advantage over simpler force feedback was statistically clear in one pressing condition, but did not hold across all tested conditions. The findings remain a preprint, a paper not yet peer reviewed.

Other gloves have improved virtual grasping, combined skin sensations with joint resistance, or adapted to different hands. These demonstrations establish narrower capabilities; none of these studies demonstrates the complete combination of realistic touch, directional forces, and comfortable movement across both hands.
missing: An integrated interface still needs to make shape, texture, slip, and yielding feel consistent as contact locations and force directions change.
Feedback still needs broader coverage across fingers and both hands while preserving comfortable, sustained movement.
Varied manipulation tests still need to establish reliable perception and action across unfamiliar objects, users, and fitting adjustments.

milestones.label: Varied tasks using both hands match physical-object benchmarks
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to compare varied manipulation with real objects and existing touch interfaces, concealing conditions where feasible. This would establish breadth beyond a single force-control exercise.

milestones.label: Results meet predefined thresholds across tasks and conditions
milestones.explanation: Evaluations would have to define users, tasks, fitting, comparisons, measures, and acceptance thresholds in advance, then report each condition. This would prevent average gains from hiding failures.

milestones.label: Users sustain comfortable movement with safe failure
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish sustained comfort, movement freedom, and safe failure across users, with defined durations, safety limits, and fitting procedures. This would establish practical usability.

milestones.label: Claims stay within tested tasks, users, and conditions
milestones.explanation: Claims would have to stay within demonstrated conditions, with specialized remote uses validated as complete systems. This would keep successful tests from being mistaken for universal realism.

uncertain: Which combinations of skin sensations and movement forces reliably guide action across different users and tasks?
What task coverage, concealed comparisons, exposure durations, and acceptance thresholds would establish sufficient breadth?
Whether N2D's benefits hold in independent studies remains unresolved.

page.title: Bimanual tactile and kinesthetic feedback
page.definition: A wearable interface would give both hands tactile feedback (skin sensations) and kinesthetic feedback (forces resisting or moving fingers) indistinguishable from handling matched physical objects. It would convey shape, texture, compliance (deformation under force) and slip during virtual or remote manipulation without a fixed mechanical attachment to the environment.

goal.need: In 16 participants, planar glove feedback reduced teleoperated pressing errors relative to vision alone. The three-finger device weighed 562 g excluding its battery and did not reflect finger-spreading forces. These results connect force information to manipulation accuracy while identifying coverage and mass constraints. The study, posted on 12 June 2026, is not peer reviewed.

figures.caption: N2D median absolute scale-reading error at the 100 g axial pressing target
figures.note: Within-participant comparison, n = 16. Values describe one experimental condition and are expressed as scale readings.

statements.quote: comfortable and customizable gloves that can reproduce a range of sensations in virtual worlds, including texture, pressure and vibration.
statements.context: The passage describes the team's haptic-glove development goal.

statements.quote: deliver a full-body haptic platform, ushering in a world where virtual reality is indistinguishable from real life.
statements.context: Founder Jake Rubin places haptic gloves within a broader full-body interface goal.

statements.quote: TACTILITY aims to substantially increase the quality of immersive VR experience used locally or remotely
statements.context: The consortium's final reporting describes electrical stimulation through the skin for virtual interaction and remote manipulation; it does not specify kinesthetic force reproduction.

completion.title: Users cannot distinguish rendered from real objects by touch during varied two-handed manipulation.
completion.criterion: A wearable interface supplies coordinated skin and directional finger-force feedback while both hands explore shape, texture and compliance and respond to slip. In blinded comparisons, users cannot distinguish rendered objects from matched physical objects by touch. This applies the published haptic Turing-test concept to the hand-interface capability. No external task battery, equivalence margin, sample size or wear-duration cutoff was identified; these remain unspecified.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback applying the haptic Turing-test concept to the quoted wearable-interface goals; no outside body was found to have specified this integrated test.
completion.basis: Searches of ISO 9241-940, glove benchmark and roadmap literature, TACTILITY, Meta and HaptX goals, prize rules and haptic Turing-test literature found no integrated bimanual acceptance protocol. ISO leaves requirements application-specific. MacLean describes users being unable to distinguish real from rendered objects, without a numerical pass rule. The fallback confines that target to the stated hand-interface capability.

milestones.title: Adding fingertip skin feedback to joint feedback improves force discrimination in a glove.
milestones.criterion: Use Baik et al.'s Measurement 3: compare joint feedback alone with joint plus fingertip skin feedback on the index finger. The reference is 0.5 N; comparison stimuli are 1.0 and 1.5 N, with 20 trials per condition and comparison. The endpoint is a lower Weber fraction, the discrimination increment divided by reference force, with combined feedback. The study published on 8 October 2020 reported this result in 11 participants, with paired-test p = 0.008.
milestones.set_by: Baik, Park and Park, Section 3.3, Measurement 3; a published study-specific experimental protocol, with no registration identified.
milestones.threshold_quote: Then, we compared the force perception for the two conditions, to evaluate the additional cutaneous feedback.

milestones.title: Users discriminate three virtual softness levels above 50% chance with a force-feedback glove.
milestones.criterion: Use KinesCeTI Study 3: identify the softer of two virtual balls for all three pairings of calibrated rigid, medium-rigid and soft settings, with three repetitions per pairing. Accuracy must exceed the protocol's 50% chance baseline. In 20 participants, median accuracy was 88.9%; all pairings exceeded chance with Holm-adjusted p < 0.001. The accepted manuscript was revised on 13 April 2026; its record reports journal acceptance on 1 April 2026.
milestones.set_by: Alvarez Romeo and Altinsoy, KinesCeTI Study 3; a published study-specific hypothesis and experimental protocol, with no registration identified.
milestones.threshold_quote: The hypothesis was that the system would render perceptually distinct softness levels, enabling discrimination above chance ( 50%).

milestones.title: Planar glove feedback reduces pressing error relative to vision alone at 50 g and 100 g targets.
milestones.criterion: Use the N2D scale-pressing comparison: teleoperate a robot hand toward 50 g and 100 g scale readings, with axial fingertip contact and transverse finger-pad contact; compare absolute errors under visual-only, single-axis and planar feedback. Sixteen participants performed five trials per condition. Planar feedback reduced error versus vision alone in all four conditions. Its advantage over single-axis feedback was significant only at the 100 g axial target.
milestones.set_by: Huang et al., N2D Section IV-A3; a published study-specific experimental comparison, with no registration identified.
milestones.threshold_quote: Performance was evaluated by the absolute error between the true scale weight and the target weight.

milestones.title: One wearable interface conveys shape, texture, compliance and slip during two-handed manipulation.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate both hands manipulating varied virtual objects with one wearable system providing coordinated skin and directional finger-force feedback for shape, texture, compliance and slip. This establishes integrated task execution before the real-versus-rendered comparison in the completion test. No external integrated pass threshold was found. The fallback combines developer goals with Wang et al.'s proposed bimanual glove benchmarks; that proposal supplies tasks, not numerical acceptance criteria.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback informed by Meta's glove goal and Wang et al., Section V-D; the latter proposes benchmark tasks rather than an adopted acceptance protocol.

not_found: No published acceptance protocol was found for the complete bimanual capability, including task coverage, perceptual equivalence margins and wear duration.
No registered protocol was identified for the Baik, KinesCeTI or N2D experiments; their milestones use published study-specific comparisons.
No independent replication of the N2D experiment was identified.
The supplied EStatiG full-text PDF exceeded the fetch-size limit; its institutional abstract was accessible.

results.finding: In 16 participants, planar feedback reduced scale-pressing error versus vision alone in all four conditions.
results.detail: The study used 50 g and 100 g targets, axial and transverse contact, and five trials per condition. Planar feedback significantly outperformed single-axis feedback only at the 100 g axial target.

results.finding: In 16 participants, triangular-prism realism differed between adaptive and fingertip-only feedback (p = 0.003).
results.detail: The glove combined fingertip vibration with finger-force feedback during grasping of virtual shapes. The study used one hand with a fixed virtual hand position and did not demonstrate integrated texture, compliance and slip feedback during two-handed manipulation.
results.quote:
as well as between DPA and ADA conditions for the sphere (𝑝 = .021 < 0.05) and triangular
prism (𝑝 = .003 < 0.005).

results.finding: In 20 participants, median virtual softness discrimination accuracy was 88.9%.
results.detail: All three calibrated softness pairings were tested three times per participant and exceeded 50% chance with Holm-adjusted p < 0.001.
results.quote:
Across all trials, the overall discrimination accuracy
was high (Mdn = 88.9%, IQR = 77.8–100.0).

results.finding: In 11 participants, adding fingertip feedback improved force discrimination (paired-test p = 0.008).
results.detail: Measurement 3 compared index-finger joint feedback alone with combined joint and fingertip feedback using the specified reference, comparisons and trial counts.
results.quote: As shown from experiment 3, the additional cutaneous feedback to the kinesthetic feedback for PIP/MCP joints significantly improved the sensitivity of human force perception at the fingertip.

results.finding: In 11 participants, combined feedback improved fingertip contact-force ratings; the Q2 omnibus test had p < 0.001.
results.detail: Participants explored a virtual surface with one hand. The study did not demonstrate two-handed manipulation conveying shape, texture, compliance and slip.
results.quote: For Q2 and Q4, the rating of PIP + MCP + cutaneous was significantly different than those of other rendering methods.
